chief_complaint: early satiety, weight loss, and epigastric discomfort
hpi_details: A 59-year-old male presents to the clinic with early satiety, weight loss, and epigastric discomfort. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he might just have a stubborn stomach ulcer or severe acid reflux from recent stress.
concerns: He is worried that losing so much weight means he has an incurable cancer like his father had.
expectations: He hopes to receive a prescription for stronger stomach medication and an urgent referral for an endoscopy.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Gastric Cancer is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management for Gastric Cancer emphasizes upper endoscopy with biopsy and CT staging, followed by partial or total gastrectomy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Gastric Cancer.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Peptic ulcer disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Unintentional weight loss with early satiety — alarm features needing urgent endoscopy.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A malignant tumor of the stomach lining causing early satiety, unintentional weight loss, and vague epigastric discomfort, often diagnosed late because early symptoms are nonspecific.
red_flags: Unintentional weight loss with early satiety — alarm features needing urgent endoscopy

must_ask.say: Have you lost weight without trying to?
Do you feel full after eating just a small amount?
How long has this been going on, and is it getting worse?
Have you noticed black stools or vomited any blood?
Does stomach cancer run in your family?

history.answer: I've been losing weight without trying, and lately I feel completely full after eating just a few bites.
I've lost about 6 kilograms over the past two months, and my pants have become noticeably loose around the waist.
No, I haven't been dieting, skipping meals intentionally, or exercising more than usual.
My appetite has dropped significantly because I just cannot stomach normal-sized meals anymore.
Yes, after just three or four spoonfuls of food, I feel completely stuffed and unable to take another bite.
I have a persistent dull discomfort right in the upper middle part of my belly that has been gradually getting worse.
I don't have severe heartburn or acid reflux, and I haven't thrown up.
No, swallowing feels completely normal and food doesn't feel stuck in my chest or throat.
I go once a day as usual. I haven't seen any black, sticky, tar-like stools or bright red blood.
No diarrhea, and my stool has not looked pale, greasy, or difficult to flush.
No, I haven't felt my heart racing, I don't feel unusually hot, and my hands don't shake.
No excessive thirst, and I am not drinking or urinating more often than usual.
No, I haven't had any fevers, chills, or night sweats that soaked my clothes.
No coughing, phlegm, or coughing up blood at all.
I haven't felt any new lumps or swollen glands in my neck, collarbone, or armpits.
Yes, I have been feeling drained and exhausted throughout the day for the past several weeks.
I feel worried and anxious about these symptoms, but I am not feeling depressed or disinterested in life, and I sleep alright.
I'm terrified that dropping so much weight means I have stomach cancer like the kind that took my father.
history.topic: Fear of weight gain and purging

history.answer: I live with my wife, she cooks our daily meals, we have no financial difficulties, and my teeth are in good shape.
I had an upper endoscopy about four years ago during a routine checkup, and they only mentioned mild gastritis back then.
No, I have never had tuberculosis, and I have not been in contact with anyone who had it.
I thought maybe I just developed a bad stomach ulcer or severe reflux from all the stress lately.
I'm terrified that dropping so much weight means I have stomach cancer like the kind that took my father.
I'm hoping you can give me some stronger stomach medicine and refer me for a scope to see what's going on inside.
I don't have any chronic medical conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes.
I have never undergone surgery or been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter painkillers, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two glasses of beer once a month at most.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.6°C; weight is down 6 kg compared to the previous year.
Mild conjunctival pallor noted bilaterally; sclerae are non-icteric.
No palpable cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy.
Thyroid gland is normal in size and non-tender, with no palpable nodules.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezing, rales, or crackles.
Abdomen is flat and symmetrical with no visible distension, peristalsis, or surgical scars.
Normal normoactive bowel sounds heard in all four quadrants.
Mild vague tenderness on deep palpation of the epigastrium without voluntary guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness; no discrete mass palpated.
Liver edge and spleen tip are not palpable beneath the costal margins.
No palpable rectal shelf or intraluminal mass; brown stool on glove without visible blood or melena.
